utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff, we've been given a copy, we understand it, of the Vance Plan, an extract from a book. We'll give it an exhibit number. The next exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This will be Prosecutor's Exhibit 355.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you for that.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honours, we also provided the list of the 14 witnesses. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Examined by Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness. Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: M. BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yesterday, you mentioned the Colonel Smiljanic and his role in providing weapons.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: With the help of the usher, I would like to put to the witness tab 111 of Exhibit 352. And it's actually a letter by Colonel Dusan Smiljanic regarding various matters, including the Martic arrest, of the 15th of October, 1994.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have an opportunity to review this letter while you had your conversations with the Prosecutor in The Hague?

utterances.speaker: M. BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In relation to the letterhead and the stamp used in this letter and the signature, are they authentic for that time?

utterances.speaker: M. BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They are.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you able to identify the signature of Mr. Smiljanic or are you not familiar with it?

utterances.speaker: M. BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not familiar with the signature.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In relation to the contents of this letter, I would like to direct you to page 2. It's page 2 in the English, and I assume it's also page 2 in the Serbian version. We have highlighted some paragraphs for you in blue, and I would like you to turn to the first blue mark, and it says here: "I illegally established links with leading figures in the SDS in the Lika, Banija, Kordun, and Banja Luka area with a group of OB security organs and military police at the end of April and the beginning of May, and I began the illegal distribution of arms to Serbian people..." And it continues: "This action continued until the beginning of June 1991..." Can you -- is that correct? Did it happen in that time period in the way described in this paragraph?

utterances.speaker: M. BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: May I raise a matter here? Isn't preferable for the witness to give evidence about it rather than commenting on someone else's letter which contains much more detail and information, the authenticity of which cannot be proved through this witness? Isn't it better for him just to give his evidence on the subject about the matter?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He can comment on the letter if he has knowledge about it. It's a question of weight, isn't it, as to how much weight one can give a comment of that sort as opposed to the evidence which he chooses to give or he can give?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: As I understood it, he had no knowledge of the letter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No, but he has knowledge of the events, which is --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. What I'm --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: -- the part of the evidence which is important.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: What I'm saying is isn't it better that he gives evidence about the event rather than in this form?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff, you've heard that comment. If you want to expand the witness's evidence on this point, of course you can.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, actually, yesterday the witness has already mentioned that through Mr. Smiljanic, weapons could be ordered, and he also mentioned that it was done through a place in the Bihac airport region. So -- but I can, of course, let him give more details on the matter. I actually thought only to confirm what he said yesterday on this matter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were weapons organised through Mr. Smiljanic in the time period from April to June 1991, and also later on; and if so, in which way was it done?

utterances.speaker: M. BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know specifically for July and August 1991, in such a way that, from my own personal knowledge, Colonel Smiljanic himself offered his services for the procurement of weapons for the Serbs in Krajina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you said he offered his services, how did he do that? What did he actually suggest he could do?

utterances.speaker: M. BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That we should address him for any needs in weapons, and he, or rather, General Nikola Uzelac, the so-called Little Uzelac, the commander of the Zagreb Corps, needed volunteers for tanks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does that mean Mr. Smiljanic asked you to organise - you in the Krajina, not you personally - organise tank crews?

utterances.speaker: M. BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Volunteers who would join tank crews.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did the authorities in the Krajina do that? Did you organise tank crew members?

utterances.speaker: M. BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Efforts were made along those lines. To what extent they were successful, I don't know for sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in relation to the weapons, still in relation to the weapons, when you had requests to make to Mr. Smiljanic, how would that be done in practical terms? What would you do? Would you give him lists? Can you explain it in practical terms what actually happened?

utterances.speaker: M. BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Men would go to see him who would order weapons, and they -- he would provide them for them from the warehouse and then they would distribute them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you say "warehouse," where was the warehouse?

utterances.speaker: M. BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know specifically about the warehouse in Zeljava, which is a place close to Bihac airport, which was the place of delivery, for three deliveries of such weapons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in which time period did these three deliveries take place?

utterances.speaker: M. BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the end of July and the beginning of August 1991.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In relation to the letter, I would like to refer you now to the second blue mark in the letter. It's on page 3. And it starts with: "Arming the Serbian people," and refers to the time period up to the end of 1991. And it also says here: "Besides this, I also had connections with the Defence Ministry of the Republic of Serbia, given that ministry's then role in conducting the arms struggle." What role did the MOD Serbia have in that arms struggle of the people in the Krajina?

utterances.speaker: M. BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am aware of the logistics support it provided.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which logistics support did the Ministry of Defence of Serbia provide, and how was that done?

utterances.speaker: M. BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In materiel and equipment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how was that done? In which way, in practical terms?

utterances.speaker: M. BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Men whose duty it was to do that went there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And which persons went there? Or do we need to go into private session for this?

utterances.speaker: M. BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that the president of the government at the time went on a number of occasions, that is, the prime minister. I know of that specifically.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At what times did the prime minister go there? Can you tell us the approximate dates?

utterances.speaker: M. BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know of at least one or two occasions in September, and at least one occasion in November, 1991.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And to whom did the prime minister then speak when he went there?

utterances.speaker: M. BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To General Simovic, the Minister of Defence of the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how did then the deliveries arrive for equipment and the other things? How did the deliveries arrive? How was that organised?

utterances.speaker: M. BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Technically, I don't know how. I just know that it did arrive.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would like to refer you now to the next blue marker, and I will quote from the letter: "Given the great opposition and problems in forming the Brigade, especially in the Lika area and part of Banija in September 1991, I organised meetings of the most advanced reserve officers and the then representatives of the authorities in Gracac and Vrhovine, at which the current president of the RSK, Milan Martic, was present. Following these meetings, a brigade was formed in Gracac, Udbina, Vrhovine, and Plaski. On the afternoon of the same day, I travelled to Novi Grad with Milan Martic intending to resolve some questions about the final capture of Kostajnica. On returning from Novi Grad, we were arrested in Otoka village, as you are aware." Sir, did you know about such meetings with reserve officers to organise the brigade in that region?

utterances.speaker: M. BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have heard of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was the prime minister of SAO Krajina present during such meetings?

utterances.speaker: M. BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would like to refer you now to the next chapter in the letter which is marked, and it says: "At the beginning of May 1992, I contacted General Tolimir, who was in Knin. Having regard to the uncertainty and the cause of events, I agreed with Tolimir, with the agreement of the Corps Commander, that a part of the assets and the police equipment should be transferred to the RSK," and he makes special reference to nine armoured combat vehicles. Were such armed combat vehicles -- were they actually taken over by the police, and in which way was that done?

utterances.speaker: M. BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was the takeover of such vehicles by the police.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know whether from your personal knowledge whether General Tolimir was involved in this takeover?

utterances.speaker: M. BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then in the next paragraph that is marked in blue it says: "After the famous telegram that officers and soldiers born in the territory of the FRY should withdraw (active military personnel made up 70 per cent of the VP battalion), officers born in the FRY were told to go to the VJ, those from BH to the RS, and you Palestinians from the RSK can go to Nis or wherever you want." What do you know from your personal knowledge about this transfer of personnel?

utterances.speaker: M. BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that in the month of May, an order arrived that officers originating from Yugoslavia should immediately abandon the territory of the Republic of Srpska Krajina, and people said that there were even some funny scenes when senior officers abandoned units and literally fled from the territory.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. We can turn away from the document. Witness, in this document, it also said that Mr. Smiljanic was arrested together with Milan Martic. Did you know that at that time that he was arrested together with Martic?

utterances.speaker: M. BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Private session, please. 8 [Private session] [Confidentiality lifted by order of the Chamber]

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in private session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which information did you get in relation to the arrest of Milan Martic, who informed you, and what were your actions then?

utterances.speaker: M. BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was informed by one of the assistants of Milan Martic - his name is Nikola Manovic - who came and told me that Martic had been arrested in Otoka close to Bosanska Krupa, and he also said that I should call up Karadzic and inform him. I also had several telephone conversations with other persons in than connection.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: With whom did you, in addition to Karadzic, speak?

utterances.speaker: M. BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I also spoke to Martic on one occasion from the police station in Otoka, and I think there were some people from Banja Luka who were there from the army, and there were quite a number of telephone communications in that connection. And also, we had round-the-clock night duty in connection with that incident.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Could we have the date, please, of this roughly?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us when Martic was arrested?

utterances.speaker: M. BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was between the 8th and 9th or the 9th and 10th of September, 1991. That is, between two of Wijnaendts's visits to Knin between the 9th and 11th of September, 1991.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "The 7th and 11th." Interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that you spoke to Milan Martic personally. Could you speak with him while he was still under arrest in Otoka?

utterances.speaker: M. BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He called from the police station.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you mentioned that you had a number of telephone conversations with some people in Banja Luka who were from the army. Could you be more precise who that was, and did you call them or did they call you?

utterances.speaker: M. BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They called me. It was the chief of security of the Banja Luka Corps, and someone else. I think it was somebody from Bihac who called up from the Bosnian police, or maybe somebody passed on their message to me. I can't remember exactly now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: While -- while Martic was in Otoka, arrested in the police station, did anything happen in the area in Otoka that alerted you and other people?

utterances.speaker: M. BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There may have been one day's difference or several hours. I can't judge exactly now. But another event occurred which upset the population in Otoka, and that prompted the inhabitants of that place of Muslim ethnicity to block Martic. I heard that they had thrown his car into the water, and then the police from Otoka saved him from the crowd and took him to the police station. So this was an event that had disturbed the population prior to his arrest -- rather, that was the reason he was arrested and taken to the police station.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you speak about the people that were upset, are you speaking of -- of which ethnic group do you speak?

utterances.speaker: M. BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of the Muslim ethnic group.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Muslims gather around the police station, and did they pose a threat to the safety of Mr. Martic?

utterances.speaker: M. BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard that they did rally, and that this rally went on for a long time. And there were fears that the Bosnian police would hand Martic over to Croatia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was Martic released at some point in time, and who arranged for this?

utterances.speaker: M. BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was, through the direct involvement of the Yugoslav People's Army and through intervention from Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who intervened from Belgrade, and how do you know about it?

utterances.speaker: M. BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Karadzic informed me about it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what did he tell you?

utterances.speaker: M. BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He said that he had spoken to Milosevic and with representatives of the army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How was Mr. Martic taken out from Otoka? Do you know that? In which way was that done, practically?

utterances.speaker: M. BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was by helicopter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where was he taken?

utterances.speaker: M. BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To Knin.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you speak with him afterwards, and did he describe what had happened?

utterances.speaker: M. BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There was a lot of talk about it, about this event, after it. It was a major media event. A whole campaign was made out of it. Martic was turned into a hero.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honours, we can go into open session again.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: With the help of the usher, I would like to put to the witness the transcript of an intercepted conversation, tab 27 of Exhibit 353.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I need to speak to the legal officer, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have an opportunity to listen in to a conversation between Dobrica Cosic and Radovan Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: M. BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you identify -- did you recognise the voices of the two?

utterances.speaker: M. BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. Karadzic and Cosic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you familiar with the voice of Dobrica Cosic?

utterances.speaker: M. BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I talked to him personally on several occasions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was his position?

utterances.speaker: M. BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was a writer, a member of the Serbian Academy of Science and Art, and later on president of the Federal Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: For the usher, could we please put on the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. ELMO the English version and, in particular, the first marked passage.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Witness, if you look into your Serbian version, there is a first on page 3. It should be on page 3. There is a marked version. The marked version of page 3. And let me read. Mr. Radovan Karadzic says: RADOVAN KARADZIC: Because they wanted to get Knin involved too, and so on, I told them not to do anything like that at all. Cosic then: DOBRICA COSIE: Of course, of course. And then: RADOVAN KARADZIC: This Milan guy has just made a stupid mistake, and then my guys ... here, I've just spoken with the vice Premier, he's our man, about this drill in Drvar. And then Cosic asks: DOBRICA COSIC: What drill? RADOVAN KARADZIC: Well, they conducted a drill today in Drvar, with their, um ... unit, a hundred and fifty battalion, one hundred and fifty special forces troops. Witness, do you know from your own knowledge whether there was a drill in Drvar of a unit and who did that?

utterances.speaker: M. BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a drill by the special police force in Knin in the month of July, 1991.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does that mean the special police force of Milan Babic [sic] conducted an exercise in Drvar?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Isn't it Milan Martic?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Milan Martic. Yes. Milan Martic, yes. Milan Martic. I made a mistake. Sorry. Milan Martic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Did --

utterances.speaker: M. BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right, yes, Milan Martic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, do you have any idea when this dialogue took place?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let the witness answer the Judge's question first.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Did you follow the question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This exercise took place in June 1991, and that's when this conversation was held.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, it doesn't say here -- in the text itself, it doesn't say "Milan Martic." It just says "Milan." There's no surname. So on the basis of what grounds is he able to say that, which Milan is meant, whether it's Milan Martic or Milan Babic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. We can have a discussion about that in due course. He can be asked. But the troubling matter is this: We've got this arrest in September, and this transcript seems to be dated the 8th of June. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: So we're going back to June now.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: We are actually having one incident preceding this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: The witness had referred to the fact that Martic was operating, and I actually have organised it to have that whole incidence and how it is connected.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, then I would like to clarify a matter with you. Did Milan Martic organise this drill in Drvar?

utterances.speaker: M. BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. Milan Martic took out the unit, about 100, 150 men, and he publicly held this drill in Drvar. This was common knowledge through the media as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would like to refer you now to the next marked passage, and if the usher would put the English version, page 4 of the transcript, here. Mr. Karadzic and Mr. Cosic are discussing the border crossing, and it says: RADOVAN KARADZIC: And most concretely here, say, it could cause the Bosnian MUP to control their border crossing more intensely. DOBRICA COSIC: Of course, anything could happen. RADOVAN KARADZIC: Well, I can't prevent that, and that is the only place where they can be helped, through, which... And then Radovan Karadzic also says: "That's where their food supplies are going through, their blankets and so on. And then, the only border which he should have spared of incidents, he is making stupid mistakes there." Did the fact that Mr. Martic organised an exercise in that region, Drvar, did that really endanger the supply routes to the Krajina?

utterances.speaker: M. BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it did not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were blankets -- reference is made here to food supplies and blankets. Were also weapons transported this route?

utterances.speaker: M. BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. Yes, it was the only entrance towards the Dalmatia and Lika part of the SAO Krajina, this entrance through Yugoslav territory.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: We can turn now to the next intercept, and that's actually an intercept that needs to be played, at least in part. And I would request to have that played in private session, for an obvious reason. Your Honour, I forgot to tell you: It's tab 12 in the intercept binder, Exhibit 353. 15 [Private session] [Confidentiality lifted by order of the Chamber]

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in private session.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Can we hear the -- it's track 8.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If you could tell the page first.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. What you will hear is, in the English translation, page 2, 3, 4, and a little bit of page 5, and it starts with: "I've just heard from Belgrade ..."

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: SECOND MALE VOICE: I've just heard from Belgrade that they said something had happened in Otoka. THIRD MALE VOICE: Where is Otoka? SECOND MALE VOICE: Next to Bosanska Krupa. THIRD MALE VOICE: They've just now been telling me too. I replied that we didn't know whether they were special forces from Krajina or not. We don't know. We know, for example, that there are members of the Croatian MUP calmly strolling around Mostar and Capljina, but no one has ever arrested them. SECOND MALE VOICE: Were these men of mine in uniform then? THIRD MALE VOICE: They were allegedly in uniform and they took three men. Then others came in lorries. They took them away by force and left. No one knows, I can't, we have no information that they were your men. SECOND MALE VOICE: Aha. THIRD MALE VOICE: We don't know whether they were yours or not. Anyone could have put on a uniform and messed around you see. SECOND MALE VOICE: I don't know. I'm surprised that they told me they were seen there and that a journalist from Belgrade television was arrested and some arrests were made of these men. THIRD MALE VOICE: But they allegedly came in another lorry and freed them. Do you know what I think Milan? That it's provocation, they want to provoke the blocking of roads in that area by this means. SECOND MALE VOICE: Aha. THIRD MALE VOICE: So that we can't deliver blankets and medicine to you, you understand? SECOND MALE VOICE: Yes, yes. THIRD MALE VOICE: Someone should strongly deny that they were your men, because we don't believe at all that they were yours. SECOND MALE VOICE: I have no idea whether any of my men were there tonight, I was surprised when they told me. THIRD MALE VOICE: Yes, yes. SECOND MALE VOICE: And I'm checking, but no one has told me yet. I don't know. There is no information on anything. THIRD MALE VOICE: Who called you from Belgrade? SECOND MALE VOICE: From the television. THIRD MALE VOICE: Yes. SECOND MALE VOICE: They called me about their journalist. THIRD MALE VOICE: Yes, yes. SECOND MALE VOICE: And said that there had been demonstrations and that arrests had been made there. THIRD MALE VOICE: See to it over there that some fool doesn't send in a platoon or something because all they would try to do is block the roads towards SAO Krajina to prevent us from getting there when we need to or something like that. SECOND MALE VOICE: Yes, yes. THIRD MALE VOICE: That thing in Krupa is one half the municipality, but about 30 per cent are Serbs. However, the Serbian territory is large over there on this side of the river. SECOND MALE VOICE: Yes, yes. THIRD MALE VOICE: However, they are certainly using this so they can criticise Serbian officials here and block ... and take steps to block these people and push the Muslims into an alliance with the Croats and war. SECOND MALE VOICE: Yes, yes. THIRD MALE VOICE: So please keep a tight reign on discipline over there, please, both you and Martic, don't allow any fool to do something under any circumstances. SECOND MALE VOICE: There's no reason on our side, not a chance. THIRD MALE VOICE: Then you can say that you're 100 per cent sure that that is not correct, that they were not your people. SECOND MALE VOICE: Yes, yes. THIRD MALE VOICE: And it is quite likely that someone has dressed up like that and is messing around you understand. SECOND MALE VOICE: Yes, everyone wears camouflage uniforms. THIRD MALE VOICE: Yes, it is very likely. You should immediately make an announcement. First check that they were not your men, and if they're not, not then ... SECOND MALE VOICE: I don't know whether they're my men. THIRD MALE VOICE: Yes, yes. SECOND MALE VOICE: I don't know, but no one tells me, so I've been checking. THIRD MALE VOICE: Introduce the strictest discipline because they will now use everything they can to accuse use us before Europe since Tudjman will lose if this continues. SECOND MALE VOICE: Yes, yes. THIRD MALE VOICE: Both Genscher and Tudjman will lose and the only thing worth their while is to prove that the Serbs and the army are attacking them, and not the other way around yes. Because journalists have already testified in the French and English press that the Croats are the first to attack. SECOND MALE VOICE: Yes, yes. THIRD MALE VOICE: And it is obvious that war suits them. SECOND MALE VOICE: We have no reason, absolutely none, neither reason nor need to pass, nor for my men to pass through there. THIRD MALE VOICE: Please make sure that some fool hasn't acted on his own initiative and then prepare a statement that you had no reason nor is it true that they were there. We over here shall say it is not certain that they were from the SAO Krajina but it is certain that Mostar and Capljina are full of special forces from the Croatian MUP who are strolling around Mostar freely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, whose two voices can we hear?

utterances.speaker: M. BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My voice and the voice of Radovan Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have this conversation with Mr. Karadzic, and when?

utterances.speaker: M. BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. After the 7th. That means on the 8th. I assume it was on the 8th, the 8th of September, 1991.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Had people from the Krajina been arrested, as discussed here? Do you know who was arrested?

utterances.speaker: M. BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there was an incident that took place, and I spoke about it a moment ago, before Martic was actually arrested. There was some sort of incident in Otoka, in Bosanska Krupa.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did it endanger the supply routes? Did -- Mr. Karadzic and you are discussing the effect that these things may have on the supply routes, and especially, it is said, so that the delivery of blankets and medicine would be received. Did he really mean delivery of blankets and medicine, or what were you actually talking about with him?

utterances.speaker: M. BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He meant weapons. Nobody would have blocked it for blankets or the like, medicines.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. I would like now to turn to the --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, this exhibit needs to be under seal. I would like now to turn to the next intercept, and it's tab 14 in the intercept binder. And of course we can go into open session again.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: It's track 9, for the technical booth. Can we please have that played. And beforehand, I have to tell you: In the English version, it starts on page 1, with the sentence: "I have an information, I don't know whether it's true, that Martic was arrested," and it ends on page 2 with the sentence: "It is all scenario that they prepared."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before that, I have a question. Mr. Witness, was it also popular among the politicians to call weapons as blankets or medicines or something like that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes. It was moderately coded, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What else were the weapons called other than blankets and medicines?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Planks, wooden boards. That was the first term used. Flour, sugar, batteries.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. We could play now the intercept, the part of it.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: JS: I have a piece of information, I don't know whether it's true, that Martic was arrested somewhere in Bosanska Krupa. RK: No, no, it's not Martic, but Martic's men allegedly, three Martic men were arrested, and then a truckload of Martic men came and liberated -- those three Martic men and allegedly some Television Belgrade journalist in some ... JS: Martic wasn't there. RK: No, no, Martic wasn't there. But I just called Babic, he says he has no knowledge that any of their men were there. I think it is a provocation, that it is them, we will deny it resolutely. We can also affirmatively prove that there is a lot of MUP Croatia men in Capljina and Mostar walking around freely, and no one can prove that Martic's men were there because there is no information that they were there or that they needed to go there, to go through Krupa. Someone wants to close the roads to SAO Krajina. JS: Yes, yes, want to close roads, correct. RK: And they're using, they're using provocation and want to close the roads. I think it's them, they need a crisis and I think they Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. staged it all. JS: Staged, right. RK: Yes, and the arrival of that truck. Hello. JS: Yes, yes, I can hear you. RK: The arrival of that truck and everything else, the kidnapping and it wouldn't be possible, I think it's all lies and staged. It's all staged because Babic has no information about it, he investigated whether any groups went anywhere, and there's nothing about any of that. They had no need to go there otherwise and they should be told not to go anywhere in Bosnia because in our municipalities we keep things in our own hands, no need for everyone to come anywhere. JS: Yes, yes they won't, won't come, nor do they have a need to. RK: They have no need to come at all. Those are not Martic's men for sure but they need a crisis and drama and so on. He wants to internationalise, Alija Izetbegovic wants to internationalise Bosnia and therefore he shouldn't be helped in doing that. Here, I told Babic down there tough discipline should be imposed not to move, no one to move outside. All military factors should be under single command, and total military factors should be in agreement with the political factor, because we have information, we know what they want. JS: Aha. RK: They wanted to, they banged the army near Okucani and they banged ours near Okucani. They were looking for an opportunity for someone to make a move so they can fuck up the conference in The Hague. Because if a fax arrived that we moved and that was confirmed, Tudjman and Genscher would have left the conference and Croatia would have been recognised, troops would be sent there, et cetera. It's all scenario that they prepared.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, who -- did you recognise the voices of the people who spoke?

utterances.speaker: M. BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. Jovica Stanisic and Radovan Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I would like to turn now to the next intercept, and this is not an intercept to be played. It's tab 13 in the intercept binder, and I just want to discuss some marked passages with the witness. The first is on page 28 of the English, 28, in the middle, in the middle of the page, actually. On the ELMO. Yes

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, if you look at your first marked part in the Serbian transcript, it says here: K: So this information is certain. Milan Martic, make a note of this, to convey, the information, to Mr. Cengic. Milan Martic, and, Lieutenant Colonel Dusan Biljanic, one of his escorts. R: Were they all in uniform? K: I don't know how they were, dressed but anyway, Milan Martic, Dusan Biljanic, one of his escorts who is a Lieutenant Colonel, our men and Milan Boric staff sergeant were there. Did you have an opportunity to listen to this intercept while you had your conversations with the Prosecutor; and if so, did you recognise who was speaking?

utterances.speaker: M. BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I recognised the voice of Radovan Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you recognise the voice of this other person who is here called -- who introduce themselves as "I am Lieutenant Colonel Kostic"?

utterances.speaker: M. BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did this intercept refer to the arrest of Milan Martic?

utterances.speaker: M. BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was mentioned.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the Lieutenant Colonel Dusan Biljanic who was mentioned here, is that correct or is the name misspelled?

utterances.speaker: M. BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is Smiljanic. Smiljanic was there. "Biljanic" is incorrect.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And following the -- following the transcript --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, we have to go into private session for one short moment. 12 [Private session] [Confidentiality lifted by order of the Chamber]

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in private session.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: The usher can -- does not need to move it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you look into the next marked paragraph, there is a reference to you, and Mr. Radovan Karadzic says that he spoke to you, that you knew about it. That's correct?

utterances.speaker: M. BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I think the rest of the transcript speaks for itself and it needs not be addressed with the witness. Thank you. The next tab is tab 7 in the intercept binder.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, did you also listen to another intercept between Colonel Kostic and Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Open session?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, open session. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you also have the opportunity to listen to this conversation that you have now in written form in front of you, another intercept between Karadzic and Colonel Kostic, referring to 3.000 people coming to the police station?

utterances.speaker: M. BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you get information that actually 3.000 people were gathering there?

utterances.speaker: M. BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: We can now turn to the next intercept. It's tab 8, and we are actually playing a part of it. And for the technical booth, it's track 10, and for Your Honours it is tab 8, and the part that is played actually starts on page 1 with the word "Hallo," and ends -- the part we play ends on ten page -- sorry, page 10, and ends with the sentence: M: I'll deal with. I'll try to get hold of Veljko.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] XY: Hallo. R: Hallo. I'm sorry, Sarajevo calling again. It's very urgent. I have to speak to the president. XY: Just a moment. M: Good morning. What's the time? R: It's two o'clock. I'm sorry, we've been calling you all day, but we didn't manage to... M: No problem. I didn't have your phone here. R: So here's what this is about. The problem is serious. The SUP of Bosnia and Herzegovina were there - the Otoka public security station which comes under Bosanska Krupa - has detained a colonel, a sergeant, and Martic, and his escort. And now the SDA over there has probably organised a gathering of people. There are already 3.000 people with tractors and whatnot, and one can't do anything, the army, until someone from the top does something. But there will be a disaster. The Serbs from Bosnian Krajina and from SAO Krajina will rush in and the danger will be great. I mean, we won't be able to control it at all. M: Right. Aren't there any HDZ members there who could... R: No, the HDZ has nothing to do with it. The entire region is Serbian and Muslim. M: And neither is the SDA which could... R: No. The SAO is influential there, and they could top it. I'm in touch with Cengic now and I'll try to... M: They have been detained by the MUP? R: Yes, that's right. They came for some kind of discussions and were detained, and now the people have gathered there. Even these military circles don't believe it's spontaneous either. Now the danger is increasing from one minute to the next. M: Who has assembled there? Have the SDA members assembled? R: Yes, yes. The SDA too, and that colonel is there. They offered to let the colonel go but he didn't want to, and those from the army didn't allow it either. M: So, they are together, is that right? R: Yes, yes. M: Where is this exactly? R: It's in Otoka, Bosanska Krupa. Otoka is on the border towards Bosanski Novi. And now the Serbian forces in Dvor na Uni and in Knin have been aroused and they want to set off from the two directions below. M: How far is it from there? R: I don't know. I don't have it here on the map, but we'll be there in three or four hours. The aircraft can't take off now. Helicopters can't get through. And 10, 15, 20 policemen will come from Bihac, but that is nothing, nothing. The army must get involved. M: It must. How long until dawn, two hours at least? There's no helicopter. It's not possible to leave either. R: Yes, it's not possible before dawn, and in the dark it's risky business for both the pilot and the helicopter, but they have to know about this. They know about this in the General Staff, but they don't have the initiative. M: So what are they waiting for, God's blessing? R: Yes. M: It's at Bosanski Novi, you say. So Otoka. R: At the border between Bosanski Novi and Bosanska Krupa, but it comes under Bosanska Krupa. M: Uh-huh, right. R: It's a matter of minutes here. It can certainly be ... the whole of Knin is on its feet, their special units stirring and they are very, very ... they must be quickly told that they have to be released, otherwise there will be serious problems. M: I'll deal with it. I'll get hold of Veljko.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who -- did you recognise the voices of the two speakers?

utterances.speaker: M. BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. Radovan Karadzic and Slobodan Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did that conversation take place? Can you tell from the contents?

utterances.speaker: M. BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It took place between the 8th and 9th or the 9th and 10th of September, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, on the transcript is the wrong date.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you aware that Mr. Milosevic got involved?

utterances.speaker: M. BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Mr. Milosevic says at the end of the tape that we played, he says: M: I'll deal with it. I'll try to get hold of Veljko. Do you know of which Veljko he's speaking?

utterances.speaker: M. BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Veljko Kadijevic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is the basis of this? Why do you think he's referring to Veljko Kadijevic?

utterances.speaker: M. BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: So that the army would be engaged in liberating Martic, in freeing Martic from Krupa.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, Mr. Karadzic and Mr. Milosevic are discussing this as a very serious event, and they make references that the Serbs from Bosnian Krajina and from the SAO Krajina will rush in and the danger will be great. Did this actually -- this event actually cause the -- did -- was there actually danger that a war would break out if something would happen to Martic?

utterances.speaker: M. BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a danger that an ethnic conflict would break out between the Serbs and the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff. Was Mr. Martic arrested at this time, 8th of September?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he arrested on the 8th of September?

utterances.speaker: M. BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He was arrested in Otoka, in the municipality of Bosanska Krupa, in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina, or he was detained, or he was kept in custody at the police station. Perhaps that would be the right wording.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: As of 8th of September.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. The witness actually had said he wasn't sure whether it was the 8th or the 9th or the 7th or the 8th. So he couldn't be precise as to the exact day. One day or the other, the 8th or --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But let me confirm with you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I think he gave, because I asked him, and he gave a broader spread of dates. Between the 7th and the 11th he gave.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. Is that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did actually the Serbs in the SAO Krajina prepare to move in to free Mr. Martic? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: M. BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They were preparing, the special police was, from the direction of Dvor na Uni and Bosanski Novi.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We can turn to the next intercept, but it would have to be in closed session again. It's also something that we are going to play partly. And for the technical booth, it's track 11, and for Your Honours it's tab 9 of the exhibit binder, and we are actually playing page 1, 2, and up to the last paragraph of page 3 of the English transcript. 13 [Private session] [Confidentiality lifted by order of the Chamber]

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in private session now.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] SECOND MALE VOICE: Hello, it's Radovan. FIRST MALE VOICE: Go ahead. SECOND MALE VOICE: So I've informed Milosevic, and he will inform Kadijevic. It's going to be more complicated over there, there are too many people, and they have all organised themselves with tractors. They have destroyed this military car. FIRST MALE VOICE: Yes. They say that they threw them and the car into the water. SECOND MALE VOICE: Yes, but they are still in the station, isn't that right? FIRST MALE VOICE: Yes. I've just -- and they told me that they would let me speak to him in about ten minutes' time. They have now sent in two civilians, these citizens, speak to him. SECOND MALE VOICE: Aha. FIRST MALE VOICE: These reinforcements have come from Bihac, and they are now apparently waiting for a special unit. SECOND MALE VOICE: There are about 30 of them somewhere in the vicinity, but I ask you Dvor na Uni to prepare your men so that they may freely enter from the side of Bosanski Brod and prepare themselves for the possibility of taking him over there anywhere but... FIRST MALE VOICE: Are these -- SECOND MALE VOICE: Yes. Let them approach from the Novi side, from the Bosanski Novi side. Let them move up there. Let them approach freely and report to the commander, that chief in Bosanski Novi. They should say that I said they should be allowed to approach from that side with a view to taking it over while you keep the others in full readiness. Milosevic will inform Kadijevic, and the army will get fully involved. We'll bring this bloody mess with our partners to an end. We'll never forget what they did, and they'll loose a state for what they've done tonight. FIRST MALE VOICE: Of course. SECOND MALE VOICE: They'll never do this again. We'll finish with them. Fuck them. FIRST MALE VOICE: ...such a state. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. SECOND MALE VOICE: We'll finish this business with them. They have shown us who they are and what they can do, but please put all of these on full alert in the border areas in the direction of Titova Korenica so they can be received, and I think it's possible in the direction of Petrovac too, to take them towards Petrovac and then Petrovac, Drvar, Knin. FIRST MALE VOICE: It's enough to return them from Otoka, the village is ours, up towards Novi. SECOND MALE VOICE: Towards Novi, you mean? FIRST MALE VOICE: Yes. SECOND MALE VOICE: You go to that village freely, from Dvor na Uni. FIRST MALE VOICE: We have to call these persons to tell them up there. SECOND MALE VOICE: From Dvor na Uni, and tell the chief and the president of the municipality, the chief in Bosanski Novi, that it has been agreed with me that... FIRST MALE VOICE: To take them up over there. Uh-huh. Look into this, please. The Croatian MUP is desperately interested in this matter. The phones have been constantly ringing for two hours. They'll try to grab him. FIRST MALE VOICE: All right. SECOND MALE VOICE: They'll do it. It's very important that these people, they can do their duty, but to set things up for the MUP of Croatia to take him. For this reason, prepare strong forces on all routes. SECOND MALE VOICE: Position strong forces on all axes and have strong forces approach from the Bosanski Novi side trained so that they can take over and ensure that he is not taken away by the Croatian MUP. FIRST MALE VOICE: All right. SECOND MALE VOICE: Otherwise, you should know that up there both Milosevic and Kadijevic know, and that if only it were possible to hold out until dawn, then the helicopters would come in and they would... FIRST MALE VOICE: This one told me they had dispersed a bit down there in Otoka. Only the most persistent have remained. A policeman who came to help from Bihac told me this, I have just spoken to him. SECOND MALE VOICE: I don't trust them. FIRST MALE VOICE: Uh-huh. SECOND MALE VOICE: I don't trust them. They all lie. Cengic is lying, and they're all lying. Cengic has spoken to me over the past two or three times. They're lying. I mean they set it all up. They set up their malicious little acts, and they don't realise that it makes the state tremble. They don't know that you can't take the Serbs lightly. They like to turn back now, but it's gotten out of hand. FIRST MALE VOICE: Yes, yes they've forgotten what really happened in Kijevo. SECOND MALE VOICE: I ... they don't believe. I don't trust them at all, so please be fully prepared. They said Karadzic told me and -- told me that he could not give me any guarantees. Because I told Cengic I couldn't lie to Babic and tell him I guaranteed everything would be all right. I'm telling I can't give you any guarantees, and I give you full authority, as far as the Bosnian side is concerned, and especially the Serbian municipalities, to prepare everything.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, who is having this conversation? Did you recognise the voices?

utterances.speaker: M. BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I and Radovan Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did this conversation take place?

utterances.speaker: M. BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Between the 8th and the 9th or the 9th and 10th of September, 1991.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall at what time of the day it was?

utterances.speaker: M. BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: During the night.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic is actually telling you that you should prepare, get ready to take over and get involved in the takeover of Mr. Martic. Did you actually prepare for taking him over at the border?

utterances.speaker: M. BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what the police did. I was informed about that by Nikola Manovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In this conversation, you make -- you say to Mr. Karadzic: "They've forgotten what really happened to Kijevo." Why did you make this remark? What did you mean to say?

utterances.speaker: M. BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The army destroyed Kijevo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that what the Muslims would have experienced if they hadn't released Martic?

utterances.speaker: M. BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Possibly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that what you thought at that time would be a consequence of not releasing Martic?

utterances.speaker: M. BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: We can go back into open session. And, Your Honour, this last intercept needs to be under seal.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, the next intercept is tab 10 in the intercept binder, and for the technical booth, it is track 12, and we also play a part of it, and we play -- from the English transcripts it's page 15, we play entirely. And from page 16, we play only up till "Certainly suits Tudjman and perhaps Alija too."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] R: Hello. M: Hello, Radovan. I've spoken to him -- R: Uh-huh, what does he say? M: He didn't know anything. He was sleeping. He -- it was probably one of his men from the General Staff who received the information you told me. I told him I was informed that we were informed, and I presented the situation to him as being very serious. He immediately took measures, and he said he would immediately take measures. Banja Luka is the nearest place in which there are substantial forces which can deal with it immediately. It is night-time and helicopters can't fly immediately, but we'll see how to deal it as soon as it dawns. Jovica tells me that some helicopter has left to get this person. R: Nothing has left and that's the problem. I'm afraid that MUP, the Muslim part of MUP, shall hand him over to the Croatian MUP. Someone might arrange this. And then it will be war in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Then no one will be able to stop it. M: No one could stop it then. R: No one would be able to stop it then. And I don't know to what extent war would suit Alija, because he wants to... M: Uh-huh. Vajnes was with me for about 15 minutes just now, and I suggested to Jovica, since he was in touch with Milan, to say that Martic should sign this protocol on this technical ... on the supervision of the cease-fire and respect -- no one shall open fire first. R: Uh-huh, Uh-huh. M: Babic agreed to this and didn't sign because they didn't want him to say that he was the president of the government of Krajina but instead wanted him to accept him as the representative of the Serbs in Croatia who is signing this in their name. R: Uh-huh. M: So I told Jovica to say that Martic would sign and that that would be an additional reason for which he should have to be free for this to work. R: No, we'll take political advantage of this today. I have a meeting with Izetbegovic again today. They are simply heading towards a division of Bosnia-Herzegovina. We will carry out the establishment of regions and set up our MUPs wherever we are in power because what they have done is intolerable. We don't believe in any sort of spontaneity on their part, spontaneity of the gathering. The SDA has influence and power over there, and it all goes towards their ... but if the army doesn't sent a helicopter or an armoured personnel carrier as soon as possible to get the man out, then the danger will be great. Milan Brzakse has a permanent line to the MUP of Bosnia-Herzegovina , to the part that is not under our control. It is a great danger. It would be a disaster if it happened. M: I told the mechanism to tell Kadijevic that this should be quieted down. R: Yes, but we can check with Adzic what they have done? M: I was in touch with Kadijevic and he said that he would see how things stood. I haven't spoken to Adzic again this morning but I'll call him now. R: Uh-huh. Do you want me to call him? It would be better for me to call him? M: It will be better for me to call him, but you can call him too. My call needn't exclude yours. R: All right. M: Tell him things are the way they are and that I told you that I had spoken to him last night and that you were surprised that they haven't finished with it yet. R: Their colonel is there too and a staff sergeant, but I mean this is incredible. We don't at all know who is in touch with the Ustashas from the Bosnia-Herzegovina MUP, and internationalising chaos in Bosnia-Herzegovina certainly suits Tudjman and perhaps Alija too.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, who is speaking, and do you know when this conversation took place?

utterances.speaker: M. BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Radovan Karadzic and Slobodan Milosevic. This was on the 8th or 9th of September, 1991, in relation to Martic's arrest in Otoka.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All these conversations that we heard, were they actually -- did they actually occur on that same day or through the same night?

utterances.speaker: M. BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right, the night and the day, the morning after.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in this conversation, reference is made to "Jovica." Which Jovica?

utterances.speaker: M. BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Jovica Stanisic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there any other Jovica in -- closely associated with the MUP, Serbia, or Mr. Milosevic that could have been meant other than Stanisic?

utterances.speaker: M. BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about anything like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, there is a reference also made to the fact that Martic should sign this protocol. What kind of a protocol is talked about in relation to Wijnaendts?

utterances.speaker: M. BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Wijnaendts was representative of the international community or, rather, the European Community. This was a protocol relating to the cease-fire, and this was actually in preparation of The Hague conference.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There is also mention made in this -- in this conversation to a person Adzic. Do you know who, who is meant?

utterances.speaker: M. BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Adzic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And there is also mentioned a certain Milan Brzakse. Do you know who that is?

utterances.speaker: M. BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Milan Brzakse, Minister or Deputy Minister of the MUP of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. That's enough for this intercept.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I would like to put to the witness two intercepts now, just very briefly, also dealing with that same issue, and it's tab 35 and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We're still in closed session -- private session. If so, we should go into open session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We are in open session. Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I would like to put to the witness tab 35 and tab 34.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, during your conversation with the Prosecutor and while you were listening in to intercepts, did you hear two conversations between Karadzic and Nikola Koljevic dealing and referring to the Martic arrest?

utterances.speaker: M. BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you recognise the voices?

utterances.speaker: M. BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you familiar with Mr. Koljevic's voice, and what kind of a voice did he have?

utterances.speaker: M. BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. A soft voice, soft.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have opportunity to speak to him and hear his voice?

utterances.speaker: M. BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, many times.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honours, those texts and transcripts speak for themselves, and I wouldn't need to discuss them with the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The next intercept is tab 11, and we will play a part of it. For the technical booth, it's track 13, and for you, Your Honour, for your orientation, it's -- in the translation, it's page 21, starting with, "I assume that you've been informed," and ending on page 22 with the half sentence, "... as we do towards ourselves."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] M: I assume that you've been informed about this thing, I told them to inform you about Martic. R: Yes, but it was mainly Aco who did it. M: Aco Vasiljevic, that is. That's Veljko and Adzic. R: No. I understand Alija very well now, and I'm very disappointed. I had to tell him this, otherwise he said he had to consult lawyers. You don't need lawyers if there's no arrest warrant. This is not a federal arrest warrant. We don't recognise the government, and we don't want to get involved in these things. He's not a drugs smuggler. The whole thing has misfired for him now since he wanted to hand this one over to them, but now he has been saved and Alija doesn't know what to do now. R: All of this goes to show what kind of government we would be living under if we left Yugoslavia. I'm grateful to them because they are screwing us. We are who we are. M: Please, we are on our way. No more concessions to anyone. And if they want to fight, we're here and they can go to hell. We're here for whoever wants to fight and we're stronger. R: And if they want to live in peace, we're here. No one will be either better or worse off than we are. M: Whoever wants to follow Alija and fight against us can do so. They will lose and it will be a pleasure for us, but if they want to be honest and decent towards us, we will behave towards them as we do towards ourselves.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, do you recognise the voices?

utterances.speaker: M. BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Slobodan Milosevic and Radovan Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just a moment.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the transcript it said tab 13. Tab 13 is a conversation between Karadzic and General Kostic. So I don't know what it is. It says tab 13. That's what the transcript says.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It's tab 11. I don't know why the transcript got it wrong if it did. Counsel clearly said tab 11. So you can follow it, Mr. Milosevic, if you go to tab 11 and then if you look at the passage which has been played, it's been the bottom of page 21. If you look at the bottom, there are some page numbers.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. All right. This was just a technical matter, Mr. May. There is often quite a bit of confusion amongst these documents of theirs. You see for yourself that it was 13 Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. that was written here. Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know when this conversation took place? From the contents, can you say?

utterances.speaker: M. BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 9th or 10th of September, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, the date on the transcript is wrong.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And for the fairness of the record, I note the Prosecutor said tab 11 and track 13 for the audio-video unit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, in relation to this intercept, I have a question which relates to a part that was not played, but immediately above the part where we started to play - and it's on page 21, Your Honours - there is reference made by Mr. Milosevic, and I quote: M: I'll tell Goran now that he should get information on the names from your people, to call them all and then cause some trouble. Which Goran is mentioned? Do you know that? Which Goran is referred to? Can you see it from the contents?

utterances.speaker: M. BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Goran the chef de cabinet of president. It was Goran Milicevic. I think that Milicevic is what Goran's last name is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And after the text that we played there is another -- another quote I want to make and put to you. It's actually a few lines below the played text.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And it is on page 22, Your Honours, almost at the end of it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic says: M: Please give Krajisnik good instructions. Let him go to Strasbourg and get in touch with Ajga. They can go together on the federal plane. Do you know which -- what was going on in Strasbourg and what Mr. Milosevic refers to here?

utterances.speaker: M. BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some meeting. I don't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And in the context of the Martic arrest there is one more intercept, and it's tab 1 in the intercept binder, and I just want to put it briefly. It's tab 1A, I'm just informed; not tab 1, but tab 1A.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: While you listened in to all the tapes in the Prosecutor's office during your stay in The Hague, did you hear also this telephone conversation with Radovan Karadzic and again Lieutenant Colonel Kostic, referring to all -- the fact that all four are safe? On the first page there is the mentioning: "All four are safe." Do you recall to have heard that?

utterances.speaker: M. BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Mr. Radovan Karadzic says: "Excellent. Thank you very much, and many thanks to Aco." Do you know to which Aco he is referring?

utterances.speaker: M. BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Aco Vasiljevic, head of security of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honours, this concludes the Martic-arrest-related intercepts, and I would now return to some other intercepts that refer to incidents that the witness has already spoken about, in particular, international conferences.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: This would obviously be a convenient time to break. We'll adjourn now, 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Your Honour, before I turn to the next intercept, my colleague Ms. Bauer has told me and reminded me that in relation to Mr. Milan Martic, we have four outstanding exhibits explaining his position, and I just want to tender them and discuss them briefly. And can the witness be shown exhibits -- tab 50, 51, 52 and 53 of Exhibit 352. And we actually do not need to discuss them. The witness should just briefly look at it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tab 50 is a document regarding a decision to establish the Secretariat of Interior of the Serbian Autonomous Region of Krajina from January 1991. Witness, this document is not signed. Was it passed? Was a decision --

utterances.speaker: M. BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the next tab, 51, is appointment of Martic as Secretary of Interior in January of 1991; tab 52 are the minutes of the Executive Council related to these decisions; and tab 53 is the decree on internal organisation of the Secretariat of Internal Affairs from January 1991. You would not need to look into these exhibits, just to -- could you confirm the authenticity of these documents?

utterances.speaker: M. BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they are authentic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: That should be enough for the documents. Your Honours, when we tried to play this intercept -- this is the intercept that we tried to play, when we gave it up for a while. That's the intercept where there was quite some noise in the beginning, and I have to say that we were not able to actually reduce the noise, but I have to tell you that it's only lasting for a brief period. And for some technical reason I cannot explain, this noise cannot -- this part of the intercept cannot be cut out. But the intercept that actually the -- the important section of the intercept is then understood clearly, so I would have to ask you to endure the noise and wait until the text comes. What it is is the intercept tab 30, and for the technical booth, it's track 4. And actually, the translation of the part that we are going to hear is page 1, the lower -- the bottom section, starting with: "Three months are out of question..." And it stops on page 2 with the sentence: "Milan from down there, and, and, if it's needed, Momir from down there, and, I don't know, sit for an hour or two, till..." This is the section we are going to play and that will be understandable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Could you start it?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: SLOBODAN MILOSEVIC: Three months are out of the question. I think that some things should be radically changed now, radically. RADOVAN KARADZIC: Yes. SLOBODAN MILOSEVIC: And that there is no place in the army which is pro-Yugoslavian by orientation for those shooting at its soldiers' backs. RADOVAN KARADZIC: Yes, yes. SLOBODAN MILOSEVIC: You see, that is that. RADOVAN KARADZIC: Yes, yes. What can make additional problems is that we decided to keep here, yes, to have them be late so that they cannot join them anywhere, well, I think they are having their three-day rest, and there Gligorov and this man are going to work again and so on. SLOBODAN MILOSEVIC: They have nothing more to do. Now we are the ones making the move, it's time for our move now. Gligorov and that man can do whatever they want, they won't ... the thing is clear there, we can't discuss it in detail now. They want to separate. RADOVAN KARADZIC: That's clear. SLOBODAN MILOSEVIC: That's clear and they should be allowed to separate. RADOVAN KARADZIC: Yes. SLOBODAN MILOSEVIC: Now there is only one question left, to have disintegration in line with our inclinations. RADOVAN KARADZIC: Yes. SLOBODAN MILOSEVIC: Nothing more. RADOVAN KARADZIC: Okay. They cannot wait for that man any more, because they are in a hurry, aren't they? SLOBODAN MILOSEVIC: Who are they expecting? RADOVAN KARADZIC: The first one expected by them is this man of ours. Bosnia. SLOBODAN MILOSEVIC: Well, they mustn't wait for him, no, concerning Slovenia, I would let them go immediately. RADOVAN KARADZIC: Yes. SLOBODAN MILOSEVIC: Let them go immediately, and the others as well after they have settled the issue of borders with us. And I cannot let your man, because your man cannot even bring it to you. RADOVAN KARADZIC: Yes. SLOBODAN MILOSEVIC: You do not permit him to. RADOVAN KARADZIC: Yes, yes. That's true, it's the truth for the moment being, but if ... you see, tonight we have had them shooting, they have shot at, at the uncle's windows ... they have had a burst fired at his window. These are now some trial actions, adaptations, etc. So that what is, what is, should be good to be done is to do things very quickly. SLOBODAN MILOSEVIC: We should take radical steps, and speed up things. It's a completely clear thing. RADOVAN KARADZIC: Yes. SLOBODAN MILOSEVIC: Take radical steps and speed things up, and we shall see if the European Community is going to fulfil their guarantees, if they are going to stop that violence and if they are going to suspend their decisions. RADOVAN KARADZIC: Is the issue in connection with Serbian violence in Croatia, is that the condition? SLOBODAN MILOSEVIC: Everything is inside, any violence must be stopped. RADOVAN KARADZIC: Yes. Yes. Well, I think it would be necessary to sit, tomorrow or the day after tomorrow, we from here, Milan from down there, and, if needed, Momir from down there, and, I don't know, sit for an hour or two, till... SLOBODAN MILOSEVIC: The best is tomorrow. RADOVAN KARADZIC: Nikola would like to come, as well. SLOBODAN MILOSEVIC: The best would be tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. We can stop. We can stop here. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, who -- do you recognise the voices?

utterances.speaker: M. BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. Radovan Karadzic and Slobodan Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From the contents of what you heard and what you have in front of you, can you say at what time this conversation took place?

utterances.speaker: M. BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the beginning of July, before the 8th of July, in 1991.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How do you know that?

utterances.speaker: M. BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because they're referring to the -- to suspending of the decisions of Croatia and Slovenia to secede for three months, and the involvement of international mediators in the matter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic is speaking, and we heard here that radical changes -- to be correct here: "I think that some things should be radically changed now." What was discussed -- what, if any, radical steps were discussed at that time? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: M. BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Actually, to force Croatia and Slovenia to leave Yugoslavia, and once they leave, what remains should be the new state, the new Yugoslavia that Slobodan Milosevic was making.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was this discussed at that time?

utterances.speaker: M. BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was discussed, in various ways, yes, at that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There is also the reference of Mr. Radovan Karadzic saying: "...the issue in connection with Serbian violence in Croatia ..." and he says: "Is that the condition?" What is -- was there a condition that the Serbian violence in Croatia has to stop; and if so, whose condition was that?

utterances.speaker: M. BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The European Community set the condition that hostilities should cease and a political agreement be reached in three months' time on the restructuring of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic then says: "Everything is inside, any violence must be stopped." Did he take measures? Did he take steps to stop the violence in the -- in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: M. BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the violence continue, the violence from the Serbian side, that is?

utterances.speaker: M. BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, provocations and armed attacks continued.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Private session for one question, please, Your Honour. 23 [Private session) [Confidentiality lifted by order of the Chamber]

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in private session.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the end of this conversation that we heard, Mr. Karadzic speaks about a necessary meeting, and he speaks of tomorrow, tomorrow it's necessary to sit. And then he also says: "...Milan from down there, and, if it is needed, Momir from down there, and, I don't know, sit for an hour or two." Does he refer to you? Did you actually have a meeting? Or is he referring to another Milan, or wouldn't you know?

utterances.speaker: M. BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have a meeting? Did you sit together? And who would be the "Momir from down there"?

utterances.speaker: M. BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wasn't at the meeting at which Momir was, Momir, probably, Bulatovic. I was at a meeting later, that I have already described, sometime in mid-July, which was also attended by Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
